title: Wikimedia Spain is holding its Annual Conference in Zamora to highlight the value of local knowledge
content:
This weekend, Zamora served as a meeting point to discuss free knowledge, heritage and open culture. The 12th Annual Wikimedia Spain Conference brought together, over three days at the Ethnographic Museum of Castile and León (MECyL), volunteers from the Wikimedia community, professionals from the fields of culture and heritage, teachers, researchers, institutions and members of the public with an interest in open culture. 

The event was attended by around fifty people, who over the course of these three days were able to share their experiences, knowledge and reflections on free knowledge and open culture. 

Under the slogan “Free knowledge is built from the territory”, the conference focused on the role of communities and local areas in building knowledge that is accessible to everyone. 

A significant proportion of the knowledge generated in cities and regions has yet to be documented, verified and shared online. Heritage, traditions, local histories, people and institutions are all sources of knowledge that can help to expand and improve the content available on projects such as Wikipedia.

title: A Journey to the Language Diversity Conference 2026 in Accra, Ghana
content:
Languages are more than tools for communication. They carry memory, humour, belief and identity from one generation to the next. For those of us who belong to communities whose languages are barely visible online, the question of how to keep them alive in the digital age is not abstract; it is personal and urgent. It was with this question in mind that I travelled to Accra, Ghana, for the Language Diversity Conference 2026, held from 2 to 4 October.

The conference was themed “Strengthening Language Communities in the Open Knowledge Movement.” It is a global gathering dedicated to advancing linguistic diversity within the Wikimedia community and the wider open movement. Bringing together editors, researchers, language advocates and institutional partners, it offered a rare space for communities working on under-resourced languages to learn from one another and to be heard. I was fortunate to attend as a scholarship recipient of the Wikimedia Foundation, after a highly competitive application process that opened in early 2026. This essay is my account of the journey, the sessions that shaped me, and what I carry back to my own community.

title: AI and the Future of Wikimedia: Reflections from WCNA 2026
content: During a wrap-up session for WikiConference North America 2026, a participant commented that they were glad the conference program hadn’t focused too heavily on AI. While I agree, I also couldn’t help noticing a sense of unease among participants about the rapid developments in generative AI over the past five years and what they mean for the Wikimedia movement. There is broad agreement that AI is here to stay, but there is little clarity about its implications for the projects and the future of Wikimedia. At the same time, I learned a lot about how the movement is adapting to these developments. In this piece, I reflect on what I learned in the AI and Tech track sessions and in conversations with conference participants. I decided to write down my thoughts primarily to help me wrap my head around this complex topic, but I hope it might also help some readers find answers to their questions and get involved in the conversation.

title: Two Roles, One Wikimedia Education Ecosystem: Lessons from WikiConference North America 2026
content:
What happens when different approaches to Wikimedia education connect? At WikiConference North America 2026, we explored how classroom-based learning and global community support can strengthen the same movement.

What is the difference between Wiki Education and EduWiki Hub? And why do we need both?

These were the questions LiAnna Davis of Wiki Education and I explored during our session, “Decoding Wiki Education & EduWiki: Two Roles. One Wikimedia Education Ecosystem,” at WikiConference North America 2026 on 26 September. More than 20 participants joined us for the discussion.

As EduWiki Hub Coordinator, I wanted to help clarify not just what distinguishes the two organisations, but also how their work connects to the wider Wikimedia education movement.

Wikimedia education takes many forms. It can involve university students improving Wikipedia articles, teachers integrating Wikimedia into their courses, volunteers documenting local knowledge, or communities organising educational programmes in their regions.

These activities share a commitment to learning and open knowledge, but they do not all require the same kind of support.

title: Dagbani Wikimedians User Group Hosts the Language Diversity Conference 2026 in Ghana
content:
When the Language Diversity Conference 2026 opened in Accra on 2 October, it was more than just another international Wikimedia event for the Dagbani Wikimedians User Group (DWUG). It was an opportunity to welcome language activists, researchers, educators, Wikimedia contributors, and language communities from different parts of the world to Ghana.

The conference was hosted by Wikitongues and the Wikimedia Language Diversity Hub, in collaboration with the Dagbani Wikimedians User Group as the local host in Ghana, with Wikimedia UK serving as the program lead.

For DWUG, being part of the organization of the conference was both a responsibility and an opportunity to showcase the work that language communities in Ghana have been doing.

The choice of Ghana as the first host of the Global Language Diversity Conference was also meaningful. Ghana already has active communities working around different languages, and Dagbani is one of the languages with an established Wikimedia community. The conference brought 82 languages into one space and brought together more than 100 participants over three days.

title: My first in-person Wikimania: reflections, lessons and outcomes
content:
Wikimania 2026 in Paris was my first in-person Wikimania since I joined the Wikimedia movement in 2021. Since then, I had participated in Wikimania virtually. While virtual participation makes it possible to connect with Wikimedians from around the world, attending in person offered a completely different experience. I attended Wikimania 2026 as a recipient of a Wikimedia Foundation scholarship.

Getting to Paris was not without its challenges. My initial visa application was rejected, and I was unsure whether I would be able to attend Wikimania 2026. However, the encouragement and support I received from friends within the Wikimedia Community User Group Uganda gave me the confidence to apply again. I resubmitted my visa application, and thankfully, it was approved, allowing me to experience Wikimania 2026 in person.

title: From Learning to Action: What I Took Away from the Interactive Media Seminar
content:
In September 2026, I had the opportunity to participate in the Interactive Media Seminar for Electoral Integrity in Abuja, Nigeria. The three-day seminar brought together participants interested in media, fact-checking, open-source information, and the fight against misinformation and disinformation. As a Wikimedia contributor, I found the training particularly relevant to the work I do on Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. It reminded me that the quality of information we share online depends greatly on how carefully we verify, evaluate, and present our sources.

One of the most important lessons I took from the seminar was the importance of checking information before sharing it. In an environment where false information can spread within minutes, especially during elections and other sensitive periods, relying on a headline, social media post, or an unverified claim is not enough.

I learned practical approaches to:

  • Verify information using reliable and independent sources.
  • Identify misleading or manipulated information.
  • Check the original source behind a claim.
  • Compare information across different sources before accepting it as accurate.

title: “Storms make trees take deeper roots”: The impact of Dolly Parton’s death on Wikipedia
content:
At differing times on 25 August, the world heard news they didn’t quite believe. Singer, songwriter, literacy campaigner, and overall icon Dolly Parton had died. Many of us did what we do when we want to be sure: we went to Wikipedia to verify the news. Every day, that reflex pulls hundreds of millions of readers to the site. Almost always, they arrive at Wikipedia articles that load, no matter how sudden the surge in interest. For about forty minutes on 25 August, the page did not load for some of our readers.

At around 18:18 UTC, four of the seven database servers in the Foundation’s Ashburn datacenter that hold cached versions of parsed Wikipedia pages became unavailable. Readers routed through Ashburn (much of Europe, Eastern North America and South America) saw errors and long timeouts. At its peak, MediaWiki was returning around 10,000 error responses per second.

Dolly Parton, 79, with her decades of work, was too much for any one page to hold. Editors have been trying anyway. Her English-language article had been edited more than 6,000 times before her death; volunteers made hundreds more in the hours after.

title: From India to Uzbekistan: How Butterflies Brought Wikipedians Together
content:
The Wiki Loves Butterfly (WLB) project began in India in 2016 with a simple idea: to document the incredible diversity of butterflies and make that knowledge freely available through the Wikimedia projects. Over the years, the project has grown into a community of photographers, naturalists, researchers, students and Wikimedia volunteers who come together to document butterflies, their habitats, behaviour, host plants and life cycles.

But for me, WLB has always been about more than photographs. A photograph taken during a field trip can become the beginning of something much bigger. It can find its way to Wikimedia Commons, become connected to a Wikidata record, support a Wikipedia article, or even contribute to a scientific observation. In this way, a simple moment in nature can become part of a much larger body of open knowledge.What makes this even more exciting is seeing that knowledge travel beyond India.
